subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: On Wednesday afternoon Oskar told Aiko in the library, “Essay is due Friday, but this time is different. I've read everything already.” Aiko raised her eyebrows. “That's what you said last time. And the time before.” Oskar laughed. He had even read about the planning fallacy in a psychology class, and had nodded along, thinking that it described other people. He started writing at nine in the evening, expecting to finish by midnight. By two he was still on the second section, hunting a reference and rewording paragraphs. The essay went in at 8:52 on Friday morning, eight minutes before the limit, and Oskar sat on the library steps, wide awake and honestly astonished.

qa.q: When was the essay due?
qa.a: The essay was due on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Oskar believe this time was different?
qa.a: Oskar felt confident because he had already read everything, and he treated this essay as a special case, even though he had run late on earlier ones.

qa.q: What could Oskar do differently before the next essay?
qa.a: Look at how long the last three essays took and plan from that, starting before the day the reading feels finished.

qa.q: What might Aiko think when Oskar laughs off her reminder?
qa.a: Aiko probably feels a little exasperated but affectionate, since Aiko has heard the same promise twice before.

grounding: A student who has run late on every assignment still expects this one to be different, despite knowing about the fallacy.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: The hostel common room was quiet except for keyboards at nine on Thursday night. “Third lab report in a row,” Tushar said, nodding at Ira's laptop, which held a page with only a title. Ira shrugged. “This one is tiny. Two hours.” That morning the psychology lecture had covered how people underestimate how long things take, and Ira had scribbled a note about it, then thought: not me, this one's simple. By midnight the introduction was written and the results table would not format. At 1:30 Ira was searching for how to fix a chart axis. “Two hours,” Tushar murmured from the sofa, and went to bed. The report was submitted at 6:10, just before the portal closed.

qa.q: What time was the report submitted?
qa.a: The report was submitted at 6:10, just before the portal closed.

qa.q: What did Ira think after writing the note in the psychology lecture?
qa.a: Ira thought: not me, this one is simple. Ira felt confident and hopeful that this report would be the exception.

qa.q: What could Ira change before the next lab report?
qa.a: Add up how long the earlier lab reports really took and use that number, with extra time for formatting, instead of trusting the feeling that this one is tiny.

qa.q: How might Tushar see the “two hours” promise?
qa.a: Tushar has watched it slip three times, so likely feels doubtful and a little amused, which shows in the murmured “Two hours” before bed.

grounding: A student aware of the planning fallacy still expects this assignment to be an exception.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Sangeeta, twenty, was in her final year at the agricultural college near Dharwad, and her field report on soil testing was due on Monday. Every earlier report had run late: the first by a day, the second by three. Still, on Wednesday she told Madhav, who shared the bus with her from the village, "This one I'll finish by Saturday. I know the farm, I have the samples." On Thursday the bus broke down. On Friday her aunt's buffalo got sick and everyone ran to help. Saturday she started. On Sunday night, under the flickering bulb, she stared at half a report and felt a sinking familiarity. "Why do I always think it'll be different?"

qa.q: When was Sangeeta's field report due?
qa.a: It was due on Monday.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling on Sunday night?
qa.a: She felt a sinking, frustrated familiarity, because once again the report was only half done despite her confidence.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do differently for her next report?
qa.a: She could plan from how late her last reports actually ran, a day and then three, and start early enough to absorb surprises like the bus breaking down.

qa.q: How might Madhav see Sangeeta's promise on the bus?
qa.a: Madhav might have believed her, since she sounded sure, or quietly doubted it, knowing how her past reports went.

grounding: Shows a student who has always run late still expecting this report to be the exception.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Mina had a system at university in Toronto: start each essay three days before. It never worked. Her last four had all been finished at dawn. Still, sitting in the student café with her friend Ivan, she opened her planner and wrote, "Economics essay: Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. Easy." Ivan tapped the page. "You said that last time." "I know. But this topic is one I actually like." He smiled. "You liked the last one too." Mina laughed, then went quiet. She felt a little flicker of hope, and underneath it, doubt. She crossed out Wednesday and wrote Sunday. It was the first time she had moved a start date earlier.

qa.q: How many of Mina's last essays had been finished at dawn?
qa.a: Her last four had all been finished at dawn.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Mina have when Ivan tapped the page?
qa.a: She felt a flicker of hope that this time would be different, and underneath it, doubt.

qa.q: Which choice at the end helped Mina, and why?
qa.a: Moving her start date from Wednesday to Sunday used her real history instead of the hopeful feeling, giving the essay more time.

qa.q: How does Ivan see Mina's plan?
qa.a: Ivan sees it with gentle doubt, reminding her kindly that she liked the last topic too and still finished at dawn.

grounding: Illustrates a student who knows her history of running late yet still expects this essay to be different.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
In the architecture studio at the college, it was Wednesday, and the model for the housing project was due on Friday morning. Zainab had cut exactly four pieces of mountboard.
Keerthana, at the next desk, looked over. "Zainab. You said Monday you'd be done by today."
"I know. But this model is simpler. It's basically boxes."
"Your last model was 'basically a roof.' It took three nights."
Zainab laughed. She had even written an essay on the planning fallacy for her psychology elective last term. She knew every model she had ever made had taken twice as long as she planned. But this time felt different. This time she really could see it in her head.
At 11 p.m. on Thursday, the glue gun jammed. At 2 a.m., one wall wouldn't stand straight. At 6 a.m., she was painting windows with a toothpick.
She submitted at 8:55, eyes red.
"Different this time?" Keerthana asked gently.
"It felt different," Zainab said.

qa.q: How many pieces of mountboard had Zainab cut by Wednesday?
qa.a: Zainab had cut exactly four pieces of mountboard.

qa.q: Why did Zainab believe this model would be different?
qa.a: Zainab felt hopeful and sure, because this time she could picture it clearly and it seemed simpler.

qa.q: What could Zainab do next time, given her own history?
qa.a: Zainab could plan from how long her past models actually took, about twice her guess, instead of trusting the clear picture in her head.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see Zainab's estimate?
qa.a: Keerthana sees the pattern clearly and responds with gentle humour, remembering the "basically a roof" model.

grounding: Shows a student who knows about the planning fallacy and still expects this project to be the exception, and runs late again.
